title: 1 Introduction and OSI Model
content: The OSI Reference Model Gihan Dias Overview Rationale for a communications architecture The OSI Reference Model - History - Overview - Levels Using the OSI Reference Model Why a communications architecture? Communications systems are complex to think about, complex to build Communications technologies change rapidly. How do you cope with change? Communications systems involve heterogeneous technologies Strategies for coping with complexity and change Modularization Layering Standardization (of interfaces) Protocol Hierarchies The philosopher-translator-secretary arch. The OSI Reference Model: Through the 1970s, proprietary systems were the rule In 1974, the ISO developed the Open Systems Interconnect (OSI) Ref. Model - The pieces needed to construct a network - A basis for standardization The OSI Model is helpful for understanding a wide variety of networks The OSI Reference Model Seven Layers Each layer provides a set of functions to the layer above, and relies on the functions of the layer below Each layer communicates with its peer layer on another node by sending messages back and forth. Layers Layer A Layer B Layer A Layer B Interface Peer Layers Service Protocol The OSI Reference Model: General Principles Services (functions): - what the layer does, not how it is accessed - Each layer provides a set of services to the layer above Interfaces: - how adjacent layers are to access the layer - Each layer has one interface to the layer above, and one to the layer below General Principles (cont.) Peers: - the matching layers on two systems - each layer logically communicates with its peer layer (physically via lower layers) - e.g. network layer on host A talks with network layer on host B Protocols: - the rules by which peer layers on different nodes communicate General Principles (cont.) How do you decide what the layers are, and what each should do? Each layer should perform a well defined function The layer boundaries should be chosen to minimize the information flow across boundaries General Principles (cont.) How many layers? Large enough to avoid grouping together unrelated functions Small enough to be manageable OSI Model Layers Application Presentation Session Transport Network Data Link Physical OSI Layers Application - Network applications such as file transfer Presentation - Data formatting and encryption Session - Establishment and maintenance of sessions OSI Layers (cont.) Transport - End-to-end delivery Network - Delivery of packets, including routing Data-link - Transfer of units of information, framing and error checking Physical - Transmission of binary data The Physical Layer Function: - Accept a raw string of bits and deliver it across a link Key issues: - Connection establishment & termination - Encoding of bits - Transmission of bits - repeating, or amplification to extend range of transmission The Data Link Layer Purpose: - Provide error-free transmission across a single link Functions: - Framing - Error detection & Correction - Flow control The Network Layer Purpose: - Deliver packets from sending computer to receiving computer (host-to-host) across a communications network. - Shields higher layers from the details of how the data get to their destination. The Network Layer: Issues Addressing - How do you figure out which machine to send the packet to? Routing - What's the best set of links from here to there? Congestion control - What if one intermediate node gets flooded with packets from many quarters? Quality of service The Transport Layer Purpose: - Provide end-to-end delivery, from one computer (host) to another. Issues: - Establishing/terminating connection - Flow Control - Error detection & correction - Quality of service - Multiplexing The Transport Layer Does many of the same things as the data link layer but... The two endpoints are across a network, not just across a wire. The Session Layer Purpose: - Provide a means of controlling the dialog between two end users (applications) Issues: - dialogue management (half- vs. full duplex) - synchronisation & recovery management The session layer is not often used in existing systems The Presentation Layer Formatting the data for transmission - End-systems may represent data in many ways - Looks at the structure of the data - Presentation-layer functions are today handled by application protocols The Application Layer Purpose: - Provide general-purpose network-based functions e.g.: File transfer Electronic Mail Directory lookup Virtual terminal Network management World-wide Web The Application Layer Some services are commonly used by many applications. Commonly used ones have been standardised The OSI Reference Model in Perspective The osi rm. describes one way of dealing with the issues and the complexity of data communications. Implementations may or may not conform to the OSI way, e.g.: - tcp/ip - sna - wap tcp/ip. Model Application Transport Internet Data Link Physical Differences Between the tcp/ip. Model and the OSI Model tcp/ip. does not include the physical, session and presentation layers - Physical layer is needed, and provided outside tcp/ip.  Functions of Session and Presentation layers are also needed - Provided by other layers (Transport / Application) Why is tcp/ip. popular? TCP/IPs strengths include: Runs on everything - Supercomputers, PCs, PDAs, phones Has consistent APIs Has a strong track record Less complex than OSI The Internet and World-Wide Web

In pure aloha,. frames are transmitted at completely arbitrary times. Carrier Sense Multiple Access CSMA Each station monitors the channel and transmits only when the channel is free - collisions may still occur if two stations transmit almost simultaneously CSMA with collision detection csma-cd.  stations monitor channel while transmitting aborts transmission if it detects a collision waits a random period of time before re- transmitting - why a random time? CSMA with Collision Detection csma/cd. can be in one of three states: contention, transmission, or idle Carrier Sense Systems (Collision Free) Similar to Carrier Sense (collision) networks - difference is logic is used to prevent collisions Two approaches: - a timer or arbiter determines when a station can transmit without danger of collisions - each station has a pre-determined timing threshold • timing can be established on priority basis - Can use techniques similar to priority slot n.w. Token Ring The network has a logical ring structure (may have a different physical structure) a token is passed around while the ring is idle Token Ring any node wishing to transmit a message must: - wait until a Free token arrives: - remove it, and send a Busy token plus message: Token Ring Tx station waits until the Busy token returns, then removes it and data transmits a Free token Token Ring needs mechanisms to set up and maintain the token these mechanisms must be - either centralised (hence single-point-of- failure) - or distributed (more complex, more expensive) Token Ring strengths: - fairer and more efficient than csma/cd. when traffic is heavy - all nodes are guaranteed a chance to transmit within some fixed time weaknesses: - complexity - delays awaiting the token Token Bus combines ring topology with bus topography nodes form a virtual ring a token circulates from node to node in sequence, but is transmitted via the bus

content: IPv.6 Based on the presentation by John Barlow http://www.grangenet.net/ http://www.aarnet.edu.au/network/design/ipv6/ Introduction to IPv6 • Design Goals - More address space - Small global routing table - Remove unused IPv4 features - Build in: • Encryption • Authentication • Multicast Historical Aspects of IPv6 • IPv4 address space not big enough - Can't get needed addresses (particularly outside Americas) - Routing table issues - Resort to private (RFC1918) addresses • Competing plans to address problem - Some 64-bit, some 128-bit • Current scheme unveiled at Toronto IETF (July 1994) Private Address Space • Led to the development of NAT. • Increased use of NAT has had an effect on the uses the Internet may be put to. - Due to the loss of transparency • Has lead to a bifurcation of the Internet. - Application rich - Application poor • Affects our ability to manage and diagnose the network. IPv6 Addresses • IPv6 Addresses - 128 bits long - Usually 64 bits of network, 64 bits for host - Network part by network manager - Host part based on MAC address - CIDR subnetting - Multiple addresses for one host Types of IPv6 Addresses • Like IPv4... • Unicast - packets delivered to the (one) addressed interface • Multicast - Packets delivered to all interfaces with that address • Anycast: - delivered to one (the "nearest“) of the interfaces identified by that address. • Specified in the v6 address architecture RFC. What is not in IPv6 • Broadcast - There is no broadcast in IPv6. - This functionality is taken over by multicast. • A consequence of this is that the all 0's and all 1's addresses are legal. • There are others also we will see later. IPv6 Address Representation • All addresses are 128 bits • Write as sequence of eight sets of four hex digits (16 bits each) separated by colons - Leading zeros in group may be omitted - Contiguous all-zero groups may be replaced by “::” - Only one such group can be replaced Examples of Writing Addresses • Consider - 3ffe:3700:0200:00ff:0000:0000:0000:00 • This can be written as -3ffe:3700:200:ff:0:0:0:1 or -3ffe:3700:200:ff::1 • All three reduction methods are used here. Types of Unicast Addresses • Unspecified address - All zeros (::) - Used as source address during initialization - Also used in representing default • Loopback address - Low-order one bit (::1) - Same as 127.0.0.1 in IPv4 Types of Unicast Addresses • Link-local address - Unique on a subnet - Auto configured - High-order: FE80::/10 - Low-order: subnet and interface identifiers - Routers must not forward any packets with link-local source or destination addresses. Types of Unicast Addresses • Site-local address - Unique to a “site” - High-order: FEC0::/10 - Low-order: subnet and interface identifiers - Used when a network is isolated and no global address is available - Possibly an endangered species Types of Unicast Addresses • Mapped IPv4 addresses - Of form ::FFFF:a.b.c.d - Used by dual-stack machines to communicate over IPv4 using IPv6 addressing • Compatible IPv4 addresses - Of form ::a.b.c.d - Used by IPv6 hosts to communicate over automatic tunnels Address Space Prefix Binary Fraction Assignment Reserved Unassigned Reserved (NSAP) Reserved (IPX) Unassigned Unassigned Provider Independent Address Aggregatable unicast Unassigned Unassigned Geographical Unicast Address Space (cont.) Interface Identifiers • 64-bit field • Guaranteed unique on subnet • Essentially same as EUI-64 • Formula for mapping IEEE 802 MAC address into interface identifier • Used in many forms of unicast address Interface Identifiers • IPv6 addresses of all types are assigned to interfaces, not nodes. - An IPv6 unicast address refers to an interface. - any of a node's interfaces' addresses may be used as an identifier for the node. • The same interface identifier may be used on multiple interfaces on a single node. Interface Identifiers • EUI-64 from MAC addresses: - MAC address:00-02-2D-02-82-34 - 0202:2dff:fe02:8234 • The Rules are: - Insert fffe after the first 3 octets - Last 3 octets remain the same - Invert the 7th bit of the first octet. • Universal/local bit Interface Identifiers • Privacy addresses: - Some concern was expressed about having one's MAC address be public. - The response was to standardize privacy addresses. - These are random 64 bit numbers. • May change for different connections • Available in Windows XP Autoconfiguration • No manual configuration of hosts to connect them to the network - assumes that each interface provides a unique identifier - Plug-and-play communication is achieved through the use of link-local addresses • Router gives /64 prefix to host - host puts EUI address on lower 64 bits Autoconfiguration 2 • Let's turn on a host • Assigns itself a link local address - Uses prefix FE80:0:0:0 - Uses EUI-64 address • Configures interface to receive addresses FF02::1, the all hosts group • Sends ICMP Solicitation Message (type 133) to FF02::2, the all routers group - with embedded link layer address • A router, if it exists, sends back an ICMP Router Advertisement message (type 134) Autoconfiguration 3 • Host adds to its address pool for that interface the prefix and the EUI-64 address - Continues to use link-local address • If no router responds, simply uses the link-local address • Stateful configurations can be done • Configurations can be hardwired - Might want to do this for servers, where changing out a NIC card might be painful • There is a version of DHCP that can be used ... Autoconfiguration 4 • No name servers passed by auto- configuration (and other things - no time server, no WINS server ...) • Other processes need to be in place to handle this - such as multicast addressable name servers, etc. Multiple Addresses • IPv6 assumes you will have more than one IPv6 address on an interface - Link local - Globally routable EUI - Globally routable privacy - Site local • Multi-homed addresses ... Problems With Multiple Addresses • If the host or app chooses from several global addresses, that choice overrides policy, may conflict with routing intentions and can break connectivity • Address selection rules are complex and controversial: draft-ietf-ipv6-default-addr-select-09.txt IPv6 Packets IP Headers • IPv6 Header • IPv4 Header IPv6 Header • Version (4 bits) -same position and name as in IPv4 • Class (8 bits) - new field • Flow Label (20 bits) - new field • Payload Length (16 bits) - length of data, slightly different from total length • Next Header (8 bits) - type of the next header, new idea • Hop Limit (8 bits) - was time-to-live, renamed • Source address (128 bits) • Destination address (128 bits) Header Simplifications • Fixed length of all fields, not like old options field - IHL, or header length irrelevant • Remove Header Checksum - rely on checksums at other layers • No hop-by-hop fragmentation - fragment offset irrelevant - MTU discovery is mandated • Add extension headers - next header type (sort of a protocol type, or replacement for options) • Basic Principle: Routers along the way should do minimal processing Extension Header Types • Hop-by-Hop Options Header • Routing Header • Fragmentation Header • Destination Options Header • Authentication Header • Encrypted Security Payload Header Implementing IPv6 • Initially, there are islands of IPv6 in the IPv4 network • Will have to co-exist with IPv4 infrastructure and hosts • IPv6 packets will be transferred over IPv4 networks using tunnels IPv4 IPv6 IPv6 IPv6 What are Tunnels ? • Encapsulate some data inside another packet. • An example, take an IPv6 packet and add an IPv4 header in front of it (next slide). • Packet size problems (maximum MTU) • IPv4 transit does not honour IPv6 header options ... Application Layer Gateways • Application-specific translator • Needed when application layer contains IP address • Similar to ALGs used in firewalls, some NATs Transition Issues: DNS • Namespace fragmentation - Some names on IPv4 DNS, others on IPv6 DNS - How does an IPv4-only host resolve a name in the IPv6 namespace, and vice versa? - How does a dual-stack host know which server to query? - How do root servers share records? • MX records - How does an IPv4 user send mail to an IPv6 user and vice versa? dns aaaa. Records • Simple extension of A records - Resource Record type = 28 - Query types performing additional section processing (ns, mx, mb). redefined to perform both A and AAAA additional section processing AAAA record: homer in aaaa. 2001:4210:3:ce7:8:0:abcd:1234 PTR record: 4.3.2.1.d.c.b.a.0.0.0.0.8.0.0.0.7.e.c.0.3.0.0.0.0.1.2.4.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa. in ptr. homer.simpson.net Using native IPv6 ... • Software upgrade to all L3 devices • Hardware accelerator changes in some L2 and L3 devices • Firewall upgrade and config. change • No immediate change to your security model (new crypto. may change trust). • Need ICMP (rate limit !) • New stuff to block (routing header ?) Software Support • Any modern O/S has IPv6 support • Most common open source tools have IPv6 support: - Apache - Sendmail - ntp - nntp - Mozilla - Bind - FTP - Ping - traceroute

content: The Transport Layer. reliable and - cost-effective service to shield upper layers from the peculiarities of the network Transport and network layers Transport layer operates in the end stations Network layer operates mostly inside the network (in routers) Transport layer can improve the service provided by the network layer - transport service can be more reliable than the network service Functions of Transport Layer Ensure data is delivered to the other end Deal with peculiarities of the NW layer - fragmentation - multiplexing - inverse multiplexing Type of service Transport Layer functions (cont.) Manage multiple connections on the same hosts Establishing and deleting connections - naming Flow control TP Layer and DL Layer The TPL has similar functions to the DLL. - connections, - flow control, - error control but Transport layer operates end-to-end DLL operates on a single link Position of the Transport Layer Layers 1-4 provide an end-to-end data transmission service - dealt with by network people Layers 5-7 use the data transmission service - dealt with by applications people The transport layer is the interface to the network for most programmers Types of Transport service Connection-oriented Connectionless Reliable Not reliable Multicast Internet Transport Protocols TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) - connection-oriented - reliable - unicast UDP (Unreliable Datagram Protocol) - connectionless - unacknowledged (at the TP layer) - Unicast / Multicast Transport service primitives Listen - wait for an incoming connection Connect - establish a connection Send - send data Receive - wait for data to arrive Disconnect - release connection Elements of Transport Protocols Addressing Connection Establishment Connection Release Flow Control and Buffering Multiplexing Addressing Transport layer connections are made to a transport address - TSAP each host on the network may contain one or more TSAPs often, a TSAP is defined by a host address plus an additional number - called a port Ports A host may have several connections (or datagrams) open at a time There may be more than one connection between the same pair of hosts These are distinguished by means of ports (multiplexing) Client-server operation Some Internet hosts provide a service (servers) Other hosts (clients) use these services Typically, servers listen on a given port - waiting for some client to connect I'm listening on port 80 and 90. Someone connect to me ... Client-Server (cont.) A client will establish a connection (or send a datagram) to the port the server is listening on I want to connect to port 80 on server www.mrt.ac.lk Client-Server (cont.) Server will hand the connection to the service process responsible. service process Port Identification By pre-arrangement - e.g., by specifying in a URL Well-known ports - e.g.: smtp - 25 http - 80 Portmapper - maps between services and ports By an application To establish a connection, the client requests a connection, which the server accepts Connection Establishment connection request connection accepted data transfer client server Connection Establishment (cont.) This will work if the network is reliable but the network may - lose - delay or - duplicate packets sequence numbers may be used to avoid these problems Connection Est. scenarios (a) Normal operation, (b) Old connection request. appearing out of nowhere. (c) Duplicate connection request. and duplicate ACK. Connection Release Both sides must agree connection is closed No data loss No waiting forever for the other side Connection Release (a)Normal case of a three-way handshake. (b)final ACK lost. Connection Release (c) Response lost (d) Response lost and subsequent DRs lost Flow Control and Buffering Sender should send data as fast as possible no data loss sender should keep copies of sent data may send up to space in current buffer without data loss may send more if willing to take risk of dropped data Multiplexing TP layer handles multiple connections to/from same host, and keeps them separate - don't want web server to get e-mail TP layer may use multiple network connections for same task - e.g. download accelerators

( Transmission Control Protocol) Gihan Dias TCP Transmission Control Protocol Most common Internet transport protocol s.ocket door TCP send buffer TCP receive buffer socket door segment application writes data application reads data TCP Overview point-to-point: one sender, one receiver reliable, in-order byte stream: no “message boundaries” each byte is numbered full duplex data travels in both directions at the same time TCP: Overview (Cont.) connection-oriented: handshaking (exchange of control msgs) init's sender, receiver state before data exchange flow controlled: sender will not overwhelm receiver pipelined: TCP congestion and flow control set window size multiplexed Use of ports allow multiple connections to the same hosts(s) TCP in action: An application opens a TCP connection to another application TCP will: split the data sequence into packets give each packet a: destination address (for routers) source address (for replies) sequence number (for reconstruction) sum check (for error detection) send the packets TCP in Action (cont.) the receiving node will: discard any corrupted packets (for which the sum check doesn't agree) request retransmission of any missing packets restore packets to original order reconstruct the original byte stream TCP Protocol Segment the TCP header (20 bytes) plus 0 or more data bytes is carried as the data part of an IP packet Max segment size is 65535-IPhdr = 65535-20 = 65515 Max TCP data = 65515-20 = 65495 Maximum Transfer Unit (MTU) the maximum size segment (frame size - frame and NW headers) that a given network can handle TCP segment structure source port # dest port # 32 bits application data (variable length) sequence number ack number Receive window Urg data ptr checksum head len not used Options (variable length) URG: urgent data (generally not used) ack: ack. # valid PSH: push data now (generally not used) rst, syn, fin:. connection estab (setup, teardown commands) # bytes rcvr willing to accept counting by bytes of data (not segments!) IPs and ports, with the SYN bit set & ACK reset (SYN packet) SEQ is set to a “random” value, x Opening TCP (contd.) Server replies with SYN and ACK set SEQ=y, ACK=x+1 Client replies with SYN and ACK set SEQ=x+1, ACK=y+1 “three-way handshake” If replies are not received, time-out and retransmission occurs Opening a TCP Connection Host A Host B Connection initialised host ACKs receipt of SYN packet time Initiate connection with SYN packet listen TCP reliable data transfer TCP creates a reliable data transfer service on top of IP's unreliable service Pipelined segments Cumulative acks TCP uses single retransmission timer Retransmissions are triggered by: timeout events duplicate acks Initially consider simplified TCP sender: ignore duplicate acks ignore flow control, congestion control TCP seq. #'s and ACKs Seq. #'s: byte stream “number” of first byte in segment's data ACKs: seq # of next byte expected from other side cumulative ACK Q: how receiver handles out-of-order segments A: TCP spec doesn't say, - up to implementor Host A Host B User types host ACKs receipt of echoed host ACKs receipt of 'C', echoes back 'C' time simple telnet scenario TCP sender events: data rcvd from app: Create segment with seq # seq # is byte-stream number of first data byte in segment start timer if not already running (think of timer as for oldest unacked segment) expiration interval: TimeOutInterval timeout: retransmit segment that caused timeout restart timer Ack rcvd: If acknowledges previously unacked segments update what is known to be acked start timer if there are outstanding segments TCP: retransmission scenarios Host A time premature timeout Host B Seq=92 timeout Host A loss timeout lost ACK scenario Host B time Seq=92 timeout SendBase SendBase SendBase Sendbase TCP retransmission scenarios (more) Host A loss timeout Cumulative ACK scenario Host B time SendBase TCP Round Trip Time and Timeout Q: how to set TCP timeout value? title: 12 Public Key Infrastructure
content: Public Key Infrastructure. Types of Cryptosystems There are two types of cryptosystems: Symmetric Cryptosytems (Private key) Asymmetric Cryptosystems (Public key) Symmetric Cryptosystems Symmetric Cryptosystems Two instances of the same key is used for encryption and decryption The key is called the secret key or the shared secret Advantages: Fast encryption/decryption process If a large key space is available it is difficult to break Symmetric Cryptosystems Disadvantages: Each pair of users needs a unique key, so as the number of individuals increases so does the number of keys, and key management can become overwhelming. For N users N(N-1)/2 keys required Requires a secure mechanism to deliver and store keys Provides confidentiality but not authenticity or nonrepudiation. Symmetric Cryptosystems Some symmetric key algorithms: Data Encryption Standard (DES) Triple-DES (3DES) RC4, RC5, and RC6 Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Asymmetric Cryptosystems Asymmetric Cryptosystems Two different keys are required for encryption and decryption If encrypted with one key the other key is used for the decryption The two keys are called the public key and the private key Public key is known to everyone (i.e., Public) but the private key is only known to and used by the owner Asymmetric Cryptosystems Public key and private key are mathematically related but no one can derive a private key from the public key However, if the private key is disclosed to the public there is no use in the cryptosystem Asymmetric Cryptosystems Advantages: Better key distribution than symmetric systems Better scalability than symmetric systems Can provide authentication and nonrepudiation Disadvantages: Works much more slowly than symmetric systems Asymmetric Cryptosystems Some asymmetric cryptosystems: RSA Elliptic curve cryptosystem (ECC) Diffie-Hellman El Gamal Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) We know that we can use public key cryptography (i.e., asymmetric keys) to exchange a secret key and then use it to encrypt messages between two parties. However, how can you check the authenticity of a public key? (remember how Charles launched a Man-in-the-middle attack during public key exchange between Alice and Bob) Public Key Infrastructure (pki) a pki. is a system that can be used to securely distribute public keys and verify their validity. A PKI is a set of programs, data formats, procedures, communication protocols, security policies, and public key cryptographic mechanisms working in a comprehensive manner to enable a wide range of dispersed people to communicate in a secure fashion Public Key Infrastructure (pki) pki. is a framework and not a particular technology PKI supplies the following security services: Confidentiality Access control Integrity Authentication Nonrepudiation PKI Operation PKI requires following components to operate effectively: Digital Certificates Certificate Authorities (CA's) Registration Authorities (RA's) Directories Many other protocols, policies etc... Digital Certificates A digital certificate is a credential that contains the public key for that individual along with other identifying information. A trusted third party, called the certificate authority (CA) digitally signs the certificate This enables people who have never met to authenticate themselves to each other since everyone trusts the CA. Digital Certificates Digital certificates are created according to a standard known as X.509 A certificate has following fields: Certificate Authority (ca) a ca. is a trusted organization (or server) that maintains and issues digital certificates. Certificate Authority When a person requests a certificate, the registration authority (RA) verifies that individual's identity and passes the certificate request off to the CA. CA constructs the certificate, signs it, sends it to the requester, and maintains the certificate over its lifetime. The CA can be internal to an organization or a dedicated organization which provides the service to others in the world Certificate Revocation List CA may revoke a digital certificate due to conditions such as: The certificate was issued to person with false credentials The private key of the key holder has been compromised CA stores a list of revoked certificates in the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) The list is maintained and updated periodically Registration Authority The registration authority (RA) performs the certification registration duties. The RA establishes and confirms the identity of an individual initiates the certification process with a CA on behalf of an end user performs certificate life-cycle management functions. The RA cannot issue certificates, but can act as a broker between the user and the ca pki. Steps PKI Terminology Issuer - Organization/server/person who issued a digital certificate Subject - Person who obtained the certificate to prove his identity Target - A person whose digital certificate is sought after by another Principal - Anything/anyone who has a public key Verifier - a person who is evaluating a chain of certificates Web Browsers and Digital Certificates Web browsers are configured to accept digital certificates signed by several CAs given as a list
